title: Heat Pump vs. HVAC System: What's the Difference?
h1: What Is the Difference Between a Heat Pump and an AC or Furnace?
description: A heat pump heats and cools with one outdoor unit, while a typical system pairs an AC with a gas furnace. Compare how each works and which fits a SoCal home.
quick_answer: A heat pump is a type of HVAC system that both heats and cools by moving heat instead of burning fuel. An air conditioner only cools, and a furnace only heats, usually with natural gas. Many homes have an AC plus a furnace. A heat pump can replace both with one outdoor unit and an indoor air handler.
body:
"HVAC" just means heating, ventilation and air conditioning. So a heat pump isn't an alternative to HVAC. It's one way to do the heating and cooling part. The real comparison most homeowners are making is a heat pump versus the more traditional pairing of a central air conditioner and a gas furnace.

How does a heat pump work?

A heat pump works a lot like an air conditioner. In summer, it pulls heat out of your home and releases it outside. In winter, a reversing valve flips the process, and it pulls heat from the outdoor air and moves it inside. Even cool air has heat in it, and the refrigerant circuit is designed to capture it.

Because it moves heat instead of creating it, a heat pump can deliver more heating energy than the electricity it uses. That's why heat pumps are so efficient in mild climates.

How is a heat pump different from an air conditioner?

From the outside, they look almost the same. The difference is inside the outdoor unit:

  • An air conditioner moves heat in one direction only, from inside to outside.
  • A heat pump has a reversing valve and a few extra controls so it can run in both directions.
  • A heat pump runs year-round, so it usually logs more hours than an AC that only runs in summer.

If you replace an old AC with a heat pump, you're essentially getting an air conditioner that can also heat your home.

How is a heat pump different from a furnace?

A gas furnace burns natural gas to heat air, then a blower pushes that warm air through the ducts. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat and has no combustion.

  • Air temperature. Furnace air feels hotter at the register. Heat pump air is warm but gentler, and the system runs longer cycles.
  • Fuel. A furnace needs a gas line and venting. A heat pump runs on electricity only.
  • Safety. A heat pump has no flame and no flue, so there's no combustion-related carbon monoxide risk from the equipment itself.
  • Cold weather. Furnaces don't care how cold it is outside. Heat pumps lose some capacity in very cold weather, which is rarely an issue in coastal Southern California.

Which is better for a San Diego or Orange County home?

For many local homes, a heat pump is a strong fit. Winters are mild, cold snaps are short and the same unit handles the hot inland summers. You get heating and cooling from one system instead of two.

A furnace and AC combination can still make sense if:

  • Your furnace is fairly new and only the AC needs replacing
  • You live in a foothill or inland valley area with colder winter nights and like the feel of furnace heat
  • Your electrical panel would need a costly upgrade to support a heat pump

There's also a middle path called a dual-fuel or hybrid system. It pairs a heat pump with a gas furnace. The heat pump handles most of the heating, and the furnace takes over only when it's cold enough that gas is the better choice.

What about ductless heat pumps?

A ductless mini-split is a heat pump too. Instead of one air handler and ducts, it uses small indoor heads mounted on walls or ceilings. Mini-splits work well for room additions, garage conversions, ADUs and older homes with wall furnaces and no ductwork.

How do you decide?

Start with the age and condition of what you have. If both the furnace and AC are older, it's a good time to compare a heat pump against a new furnace and AC. A technician should look at your ducts, your electrical panel and your comfort complaints before recommending one or the other.

It also helps to think about the next ten to fifteen years. If you plan to add solar, an electric water heater or an EV charger, a heat pump may fit well with that plan. If you'd rather keep gas heat, a high-efficiency furnace paired with a new AC is still a solid, reliable choice.

faqs: Can a heat pump keep my house warm in winter?

In most of San Diego County and Orange County, yes. Our winters are mild, and modern heat pumps are designed to keep heating well below the temperatures we usually see. Homes in colder inland or foothill areas may want a model rated for colder weather or a dual-fuel setup.
Does a heat pump cost more to run than a gas furnace?

It depends on your local gas and electric rates and how efficient each system is. Heat pumps use energy very efficiently, but electricity rates in California are high. A technician can help you compare using your actual bills.
Do heat pumps need more maintenance?
They need about the same care as an AC, but because they run all year, a check in spring and again in fall is a good idea. Keep the filter clean and the outdoor unit clear of leaves and debris.
What is emergency heat on a heat pump thermostat?

Emergency heat turns on backup electric heat strips, or a furnace in a dual-fuel system, and skips the heat pump. It's meant for when the heat pump fails, not for regular use, because heat strips cost a lot more to run.
